items.title: Emergence of the Pallavas of Kanchi
items.body:
### Emergence of the Pallavas of Kanchi

**In one line:** After the Gupta empire faded, two big kingdoms rose in the south — the **Pallavas** (around Kanchipuram) and the **Chalukyas** (around Badami) — and the Pallavas began their imperial rule when **Simhavishnu** defeated a group called the **Kalabhras**.

**Why it is asked:** This topic opens the "post-Gupta South India" chapter. Examiners love the Pallava capital, their founder, and whom they fought, so getting the frame right makes every later question easier.

**The story**

- The **Kalabhras** were an obscure ruling group who had disturbed the old Tamil order. Around **575 CE** the Pallava king **Simhavishnu** defeated them and set up strong, organised ("imperial") Pallava rule.
- Their heartland was **south Andhra Pradesh and north Tamil Nadu**, ruled from the capital **Kanchipuram (Kanchi)**.
- They were almost always at war: against the **Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami)** to the north, and the **Cholas and Pandyas** to the south.
- Under them **Kanchi grew** into a famous **temple town** and a centre of **trade and learning**.
- Pallava kings took the grand title **Dharma-Maharaja** ("great king of righteous rule").

**Why it matters:** The Pallavas created the Dravidian temple style and village self-government that the later Cholas perfected — so they are the starting point of medieval South Indian history.

**Terms explained**

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Imperial Pallavas | The strong, well-organised Pallava rule that began with Simhavishnu (as opposed to earlier minor Pallava chiefs) |
| Kalabhras | A ruling group the Pallavas overthrew to gain power |
| Dharma-Maharaja | A royal title meaning "great king of righteous rule" |

**Don't confuse:** Pallava capital = **Kanchi**; Chalukya capital = **Vatapi/Badami**. Do not mix the two.

**Remember it:** Pallavas → capital **Kanchi** → the "temple town" whose monuments at Mamallapuram are still famous.

**TL;DR**
- Simhavishnu beat the Kalabhras to start imperial Pallava rule.
- Capital = Kanchipuram; core region = south AP + north Tamil Nadu.
- Rivals: Chalukyas (north), Cholas and Pandyas (south).
- Kings used the title Dharma-Maharaja.

figure.alt: Map of peninsular India showing the Chalukya realm (Aihole, Badami) and the Pallava realm around Kanchipuram, with neighbouring Pandya, Ganga and Kalinga
figure.caption: Post-Gupta south India: the Chalukyas of Badami (Aihole, Badami) in the Deccan and the Pallavas around Kanchipuram, flanked by the Pandyas and Gangas.

keyPoints: Simhavishnu defeated the Kalabhras and began imperial Pallava rule.
Capital: Kanchipuram (Kanchi); core in south AP and north Tamil Nadu.
Rivals: Chalukyas of Vatapi (north); Cholas and Pandyas (south).
Kanchi became a major temple town and trade centre.
Kings took the title Dharma-Maharaja.
items.mnemonic: Pallavas → capital Kanchi → temple town of the south (Mamallapuram monuments to come).

items.title: Simhavishnu — Founder of the Imperial Pallavas
items.body:
### Simhavishnu — Founder of the Imperial Pallavas

**In one line:** Simhavishnu (ruled about **575–590 CE**) is the king who turned the Pallavas from minor chiefs into a real empire by crushing the Kalabhras.

**Why it is asked:** "Who founded the imperial Pallavas?" and "Who patronised the poet Bharavi?" are both standard one-mark questions — and the answer to both is Simhavishnu.

**The story**

- He **defeated the Kalabhras** and established organised Pallava rule from Kanchi.
- He took the proud title **Avanisimha**, which means **"Lion of the Earth"**.
- He was a patron of learning: he supported the great Sanskrit poet **Bharavi**, author of the long poem **Kiratarjuniya**.
- His conquests gave the territorial base on which later, more famous Pallavas built.

**Why it matters:** He is the "foundation stone" — later kings like Narasimhavarman I inherited the kingdom he created.

**Terms explained**

- **Avanisimha** — a title meaning "Lion of the Earth" (avani = earth, simha = lion).
- **Kiratarjuniya** — a classical Sanskrit epic poem (a *mahakavya*) by Bharavi, retelling an episode from the Mahabharata.

**Don't confuse:** The *founder* is **Simhavishnu**; the king who *wrote a book himself* was his successor **Mahendravarman I** — Simhavishnu only patronised a poet.

**Remember it:** **Simha**vishnu the "Avani-**simha**" (two lions) → founder-king who ended the Kalabhras.

**TL;DR**
- Founder of the imperial Pallavas (about 575–590 CE).
- Defeated the Kalabhras.
- Title: Avanisimha ("Lion of the Earth").
- Patronised Bharavi, author of the Kiratarjuniya.
keyPoints: Founder of the imperial Pallavas (about 575–590 CE).
Defeated the Kalabhras to establish Pallava rule.
Bore the title Avanisimha ('Lion of the Earth').
Patronised the poet Bharavi, author of the Kiratarjuniya.
items.mnemonic: Simhavishnu the 'Avanisimha' → Kanchi → founder-king who crushed the Kalabhras.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions of the Pallavas — Simhavishnu)

items.title: Mahendravarman I — Pioneer of Rock-cut Architecture
items.body:
### Mahendravarman I — Pioneer of Rock-cut Architecture

**In one line:** Mahendravarman I (ruled about **600–630 CE**) was an artist-king who started the Pallava tradition of carving temples out of solid rock and who wrote a famous Sanskrit comedy.

**Why it is asked:** He links three favourite exam facts — a book (*Mattavilasa Prahasana*), an art style (rock-cut), and a battle (Pullalur) — so he appears in match-the-following and statement questions.

**The story**

- He expanded Pallava power and was a many-sided cultural patron.
- He took playful titles such as **Mattavilasa** ("one who delights in pleasure") and **Chitrakarapuli** ("tiger among painters").
- He began the **Mahendra style** of **rock-cut architecture** — temples cut straight into living rock, using **no bricks and no wood**.
- He wrote the Sanskrit satire **Mattavilasa Prahasana** (a *prahasana* is a one-act comic farce).
- He was **defeated and killed by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II at the Battle of Pullalur** — the opening clash of the long Pallava–Chalukya wars.

**Why it matters:** Rock-cut temples were the first step towards the great stone temples of the south; the Pullalur defeat set up his son's famous revenge.

**Terms explained**

- **Rock-cut temple** — a shrine carved into natural rock, not built from separate blocks.
- **Prahasana** — a short Sanskrit comic play/farce.
- **Chitrakarapuli** — "tiger among painters", praising his skill in painting.

**Don't confuse:** Mahendravarman I did **rock-cut** work; his grandson **Rajasimha** built **structural** (block-by-block) stone temples. Different kings, different techniques.

**Remember it:** **Mahendra** = **M**andapa (first cave temples) + **M**attavilasa (his book); he **lost** at Pullalur.

**TL;DR**
- Ruled about 600–630 CE; expanded Pallava power.
- Titles: Mattavilasa and Chitrakarapuli.
- Began the Mahendra rock-cut style (no brick or wood).
- Wrote the Mattavilasa Prahasana.
- Killed by Pulakeshin II at the Battle of Pullalur.
keyPoints: Ruled about 600–630 CE; expanded Pallava power.
Titles: Mattavilasa and Chitrakarapuli ('tiger among painters').
Began the Mahendra rock-cut style — no brick or wood.
Wrote the Sanskrit satire Mattavilasa Prahasana.
Killed by Pulakeshin II (Chalukya) at the Battle of Pullalur.
items.mnemonic: Mahendravarman → Kanchi → the FIRST rock-cut mandapas (Mahendra Style); lost to Pulakeshin II at Pullalur.

items.title: Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) — Conqueror of Vatapi
items.body:
### Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) — Conqueror of Vatapi

**In one line:** Narasimhavarman I (ruled about **630–668 CE**) is counted the **greatest Pallava king**: he avenged his father by destroying the Chalukya capital Vatapi and founded the monument city of Mamallapuram.

**Why it is asked:** His reign is the Pallava high point, so examiners pack three facts into one statement question — the Vatapi victory, Mamallapuram, and his meeting with the Chinese pilgrim Hsuen Tsang.

**The story**

- His father Mahendravarman I had been killed by **Pulakeshin II** at Pullalur. Narasimhavarman I struck back, **defeated and killed Pulakeshin II and destroyed Vatapi (Badami)** — so he took the title **Vatapikonda**, "Conqueror of Vatapi".
- He **founded Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram)** and began the **Seven Rathas** — chariot-shaped shrines each carved from a single rock (the **Mamalla style**).
- He **invaded Sri Lanka twice** to help the exiled prince **Manavamma** regain his throne.
- He **hosted the Chinese traveller Hsuen Tsang (Xuanzang) at Kanchipuram in 642 CE**.

**Why it matters:** He combined military success, overseas reach, and pioneering art — the full picture of Pallava power at its peak.

**Terms explained**

- **Vatapikonda** — title meaning "Conqueror of Vatapi" (konda = conquered).
- **Ratha** — literally "chariot"; here a monolithic (single-rock) temple shaped like a chariot.
- **Mamalla** — "great wrestler", his personal title, which gave Mamallapuram its name.

**Don't confuse:** The **Seven Rathas** (monolithic) were begun by **Narasimhavarman I**; the **Shore Temple** (structural) was built later by **Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)**. Same town, different kings.

**Remember it:** **Mamalla → Mamalla**puram → the Seven Rathas; "**Vatapi-konda**" razed Vatapi.

**TL;DR**
- Greatest Pallava king (about 630–668 CE); title Vatapikonda.
- Defeated and killed Pulakeshin II; destroyed Vatapi.
- Founded Mamallapuram; began the Seven Rathas (Mamalla style).
- Invaded Sri Lanka twice for prince Manavamma.
- Hosted Hsuen Tsang at Kanchi in 642 CE.

figure.alt: The monolithic Pancha Rathas (Seven Rathas) carved from granite at Mamallapuram
figure.caption: The monolithic Rathas at Mamallapuram, initiated by Narasimhavarman I — the hallmark of the Mamalla Style.

keyPoints: Greatest Pallava king (about 630–668 CE); title Vatapikonda.
Defeated and killed Pulakeshin II and destroyed Vatapi (Badami).
Founded Mamallapuram; began the Seven Rathas (Mamalla style).
Invaded Sri Lanka twice to aid the exiled prince Manavamma.
Hosted Hsuen Tsang at Kanchipuram in 642 CE.
items.mnemonic: Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' → Mamallapuram → the Seven Rathas; 'Vatapikonda' who razed Vatapi.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions — Narasimhavarman I / Mamalla)

items.title: Later Pallavas — Rajasimha and Nandivarman II
items.body:
### Later Pallavas — Rajasimha and Nandivarman II

**In one line:** After the war-hero Narasimhavarman I came two temple-building kings — **Rajasimha**, who built structural stone temples in peacetime, and **Nandivarman II**, who built a great Vishnu temple and backed the Bhakti movement.

**Why it is asked:** The "who built which temple" match is a classic question, and these two kings own the Shore, Kailashnath and Vaikunth Perumal temples.

**The story**

**Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha, about 695–722 CE)**
- His reign was mostly **peaceful**, with the Chalukya wars paused.
- He built the **Shore Temple** at Mahabalipuram and the **Kailashnath Temple** at Kanchi — true **structural** temples (built up from dressed stone blocks), the **Rajasimha style**.
- He **sent embassies to China** to build trade and diplomatic ties.

**Nandivarman II (about 736–796 CE)**
- He built the **Vaikunth Perumal Temple** at Kanchi, dedicated to **Vishnu**.
- He **promoted the Bhakti movement** through temple worship and **strengthened village self-government**.

**Why it matters:** They mark the shift from rock-cut caves to full stone temples, and the rise of devotional (Bhakti) worship under royal support.

**Terms explained**

- **Structural temple** — a temple built up from cut stone blocks (unlike a rock-cut cave).
- **Bhakti** — personal, loving devotion to a god, expressed in hymns rather than costly ritual.
- **Embassy** — an official mission sent by one ruler to another.

**Don't confuse:** **Rajasimha** = Shore + Kailashnath temples; **Nandivarman II** = Vaikunth Perumal temple. Keep the king–temple pairs straight.

**Remember it:** **Raja**simha built by the **shore** (Shore Temple); **Nandi**varman built for **Vishnu** (Vaikunth Perumal).

**TL;DR**
- Rajasimha (about 695–722 CE): peace; built Shore and Kailashnath temples; sent embassies to China.
- Shore and Kailashnath are structural stone temples (Rajasimha style).
- Nandivarman II (about 736–796 CE): built the Vaikunth Perumal Temple (Vishnu).
- Nandivarman II promoted Bhakti and village self-government.

figure.alt: The twin-spired Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram beside the sea
figure.caption: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram, built by Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) — a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyPoints: Rajasimha (about 695–722 CE): peace with the Chalukyas; sent embassies to China.
Built the Shore Temple (Mahabalipuram) and Kailashnath Temple (Kanchi) — structural Rajasimha style.
Nandivarman II (about 736–796 CE) built the Vaikunth Perumal Temple, dedicated to Vishnu.
Nandivarman II promoted the Bhakti movement and strengthened village autonomy.
items.mnemonic: Rajasimha → Kanchi/Mahabalipuram → Shore & Kailashnath temples; Nandivarman → Vaikunth Perumal (Vishnu).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions — Narasimhavarman II & Nandivarman II)

items.title: Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) — Pulakeshin II & the Aihole Inscription
items.body:
### Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) — Pulakeshin II & the Aihole Inscription

**In one line:** The **Chalukyas of Badami** were the Pallavas' great rivals in the Deccan; their finest king, **Pulakeshin II**, even stopped the north-Indian emperor Harsha, and his victories are recorded in the famous **Aihole inscription**.

**Why it is asked:** The Aihole inscription (its author, its temple, its contents) is the single highest-yield fact of this topic, and Pulakeshin II sits at the centre of the whole Pallava–Chalukya story.

**The story**

- The Chalukyas ruled the Deccan from the capital **Badami (Vatapi)**, with a ceremonial temple-town at **Aihole**.
- Their greatest king, **Pulakeshin II**, is praised in the **Aihole inscription**, written by his Jain court poet **Ravikirti** on the **Meguti Jain temple (634 CE)** in polished Sanskrit.
- Pulakeshin II **stopped Harshavardhana of Kanauj at the river Narmada**, halting Harsha's march into the south — a landmark event.
- Against the Pallavas the result swung both ways: he **killed Mahendravarman I at Pullalur**, but was later **defeated and killed by Narasimhavarman I, who sacked Vatapi**.
- Chalukya kings built the great temple groups at **Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal**, the nursery of the hybrid **Vesara style**.

**Why it matters:** Stopping Harsha fixed the Narmada as the limit between north and south India for that age, and the Aihole inscription is a model of royal eulogy history.

**Terms explained**

- **Prashasti** — a royal eulogy inscription praising a king's deeds (the Aihole inscription is one).
- **Vatapi** — the old name of Badami, the Chalukya capital.
- **Vesara** — a temple style blending northern and southern features (explained in the architecture note).

**Don't confuse:** The Aihole inscription's **author** is the poet **Ravikirti**; the **king** it praises is **Pulakeshin II**. Questions often swap these two.

**Remember it:** **Aihole = Ravikirti praises Pulakeshin II**, who stopped **Harsha at the Narmada**.

**TL;DR**
- Capital Badami (Vatapi); ceremonial town Aihole; greatest king Pulakeshin II.
- Aihole inscription written by the Jain poet Ravikirti (Meguti temple, 634 CE).
- Pulakeshin II stopped Harshavardhana at the Narmada.
- He killed Mahendravarman I at Pullalur, but was later defeated by Narasimhavarman I, who sacked Vatapi.
- Temple groups at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal — home of the Vesara style.

figure.alt: Map showing the Chalukya realm centred on Badami and Aihole in the Deccan
figure.caption: The Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) held the Deccan around Aihole and Badami — the Pallavas' principal northern rivals.

keyPoints: Capital Badami (Vatapi); ceremonial centre Aihole; greatest king Pulakeshin II.
Aihole inscription composed by the Jain court poet Ravikirti (Meguti temple, 634 CE).
Pulakeshin II checked Harshavardhana on the Narmada.
Killed Mahendravarman I at Pullalur; later defeated and slain by Narasimhavarman I, who sacked Vatapi.
Temple complexes at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal — nursery of the Vesara style.
items.mnemonic: Chalukyas → capital Badami (Vatapi) → Aihole & Pattadakal temples; Pulakeshin II praised by Ravikirti, stopped Harsha at the Narmada.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Chalukya references: Vatapi, Pulakeshin II, Battle of Pullalur; map: Aihole/Badami) with standard historical record (Aihole inscription of Ravikirti, Harsha–Narmada, Pattadakal)

items.title: Evolution of Pallava Architecture — Four Styles
items.body:
### Evolution of Pallava Architecture — Four Styles

**In one line:** Pallava temple-building grew in four named stages, moving from caves cut into rock to full stone temples — and in doing so it created the South Indian (Dravidian) temple style.

**Why it is asked:** The four styles, in order, with one example each, are a favourite match-the-following question.

**The story**

Think of it as a ladder from "carving into rock" to "building up with blocks":

| Style | King | What is new | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mahendra | Mahendravarman I | First rock-cut temples; no brick or wood | Mamandur, Trimurti Mandapa |
| Mamalla | Narasimhavarman I | Monolithic Rathas + lion-headed (yali) pillars | Seven Rathas, Varaha Mandapa |
| Rajasimha | Narasimhavarman II | Elaborate structural stone temples | Shore Temple, Kailashnath |
| Nandivarman | Nandivarman II | Smaller, plainer temples — decline | Mukteshwar, Matangeshwar |

**Why it matters:** This is the birth of the **Dravidian** style (a stepped, pyramid-like tower called a *vimana*), which differs from the North Indian **Nagara** style (a curved tower called a *shikhara*) and the Deccan's hybrid **Vesara** style.

**Terms explained**

- **Monolithic** — carved from a single block of rock.
- **Mandapa** — a pillared hall in front of the shrine.
- **Vimana** — the pyramid-like tower over a South Indian (Dravidian) shrine.
- **Shikhara** — the curved tower over a North Indian (Nagara) shrine.
- **Yali** — a mythical lion figure used on pillars.

**Don't confuse:** **Mahendra** = rock-cut; **Mamalla** = Rathas; **Rajasimha** = structural temples; **Nandivarman** = decline. Learn them strictly in order.

**Remember it:** Order "**Ma-Ma-Ra-Na**": **Ma**hendra → **Ma**malla → **Ra**jasimha → **Na**ndivarman.

**TL;DR**
- Mahendra: first rock-cut temples, no brick or wood.
- Mamalla: monolithic Rathas and lion-headed pillars.
- Rajasimha: elaborate structural stone temples.
- Nandivarman: smaller temples — the decline.
- South = Dravidian (vimana); North = Nagara (shikhara); Deccan = Vesara (hybrid).
keyPoints: Mahendra style: first rock-cut temples, no brick or wood (Mamandur, Trimurti Mandapa).
Mamalla style: monolithic Rathas and lion-headed pillars (Seven Rathas, Varaha Mandapa).
Rajasimha style: elaborate structural stone temples (Shore Temple, Kailashnath).
Nandivarman style: smaller, plainer temples — the decline.
South = Dravidian (vimana); North = Nagara (shikhara); Deccan = Vesara (hybrid).
items.mnemonic: Pallava order 'Ma-Ma-Ra-Na': Mahendra (rock-cut) → Mamalla (Rathas) → Rajasimha (structural) → Nandivarman (decline).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Art and Architecture under the Pallavas)

items.title: Major Pallava Temples and Monuments
items.body:
### Major Pallava Temples and Monuments

**In one line:** A handful of Pallava monuments appear again and again in exams — the Shore Temple, the Kailashnath Temple, the Seven Rathas and the Vaikunth Perumal Temple — so it pays to pin each to its king, place and deity.

**Why it is asked:** "Who built the Shore Temple?" or "The Vaikunth Perumal is dedicated to whom?" are direct one-mark questions.

**The story**

| Monument | Built by | Place | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shore Temple | Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) | Mahabalipuram | Three shrines to Shiva and Vishnu; a UNESCO World Heritage Site |
| Kailashnath Temple | Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) | Kanchipuram | 16-sided Shivalinga; ringed by 58 mini-shrines (devakulikas) |
| Seven Rathas | Narasimhavarman I | Mahabalipuram | Monolithic; includes Draupadi, Dharmaraja and Bhima Rathas |
| Vaikunth Perumal | Nandivarman II | Kanchipuram | Dedicated to Vishnu (standing, sitting, reclining); inscriptions record Nandivarman's rise to power |

- Pallava **painting** survives in the **Chittannavasal frescoes**.

**Why it matters:** These monuments are the physical proof of the four styles, and Mahabalipuram as a whole is a UNESCO site that still appears in current-affairs quizzes.

**Terms explained**

- **Shivalinga** — the symbolic form of the god Shiva worshipped in the shrine.
- **Devakulika** — a small subsidiary shrine around a main temple.
- **Fresco** — a wall painting done on fresh plaster.

**Don't confuse:** Both the **Shore Temple** and the **Seven Rathas** are at **Mahabalipuram** — but the Rathas are Narasimhavarman **I** and the Shore Temple is Narasimhavarman **II**.

**Remember it:** Mahabalipuram → **Rathas (I)** then **Shore Temple (II)**; Kanchi → **Kailashnath** and **Vaikunth Perumal**.

**TL;DR**
- Shore Temple (Rajasimha, Mahabalipuram): three shrines, UNESCO site.
- Kailashnath (Rajasimha, Kanchi): 16-sided Shivalinga, 58 devakulikas.
- Seven Rathas (Narasimhavarman I): monolithic; Draupadi, Dharmaraja, Bhima.
- Vaikunth Perumal (Nandivarman II, Kanchi): Vishnu in three forms.
- Chittannavasal frescoes preserve Pallava painting.
keyPoints: Shore Temple (Narasimhavarman II, Mahabalipuram): three shrines, UNESCO site.
Kailashnath Temple (Narasimhavarman II, Kanchi): 16-sided Shivalinga, 58 devakulikas.
Seven Rathas (Narasimhavarman I): monolithic; Draupadi, Dharmaraja, Bhima Rathas.
Vaikunth Perumal (Nandivarman II): Vishnu in three forms; inscriptions on his accession.
Chittannavasal frescoes showcase Pallava painting.
items.mnemonic: Mahabalipuram monuments: Rathas (Narasimhavarman I) → Shore Temple (Narasimhavarman II); Kanchi → Kailashnath & Vaikunth Perumal.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Major Pallava Temples and Structures; Painting)

items.title: Administration under the Pallavas
items.body:
### Administration under the Pallavas

**In one line:** The Pallava state was a monarchy at the top but rested on **self-governing villages** at the bottom — a system the later Cholas made famous.

**Why it is asked:** The special terms — Kottam, Sabha, Urar, Dharmasasana — are exactly what match-the-following questions test.

**The story**

- **Form of rule:** a **monarchy**; kings used the title **Dharma-Maharaja**.
- **Big divisions:** the empire was split into **Kottams**, each run by officers the king appointed.
- **Villages ran themselves:** local assemblies managed village affairs — the **Sabha** looked after **Brahmadeya** (Brahmin) villages, and the **Urar** looked after ordinary villages.
- **Justice:** every village had a court called the **Dharmasasana**.
- This habit of **local self-government** grew even stronger later under the **Cholas**.

**Why it matters:** South Indian village democracy is a big theme in Indian history; the Pallavas are where it begins in an organised way.

**Terms explained**

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Kottam | A large administrative division (like a district) |
| Sabha | The assembly of a Brahmin (Brahmadeya) village |
| Urar | The assembly of an ordinary village |
| Dharmasasana | The village court that gave justice |

**Don't confuse:** **Sabha** = Brahmin villages; **Urar** = ordinary villages. The division into **Kottams** is Pallava — other dynasties used Vishaya, Rashtra or Ahara.

**Remember it:** Top to bottom: **King → Kottam → Sabha/Urar village → Dharmasasana court**.

**TL;DR**
- Monarchy; kings styled Dharma-Maharaja.
- Empire divided into Kottams under royal officers.
- Villages self-governed by assemblies — Sabha (Brahmin) and Urar (ordinary).
- Village court = Dharmasasana.
- Base for later Chola village self-government.
keyPoints: Monarchy; kings styled Dharma-Maharaja.
Empire divided into Kottams under royal officers.
Villages self-governed by assemblies — Sabha (Brahmin) and Urar (ordinary).
Village court called Dharmasasana dispensed justice.
Foundation for later Chola local self-government.
items.mnemonic: Pallava rule → Kanchi throne → Kottams above, Sabha/Urar villages below, Dharmasasana courts.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Administration under the Pallavas)

items.title: Economy under the Pallavas
items.body:
### Economy under the Pallavas

**In one line:** The Pallava economy ran mainly on **land revenue**, supported by many small taxes, Brahmin land grants, merchant guilds, and special lands set aside to keep village tanks working.

**Why it is asked:** The economic terms — Brahmadeya, Manigramam, Eripatti — are tested in match-the-following questions, so each must be pinned to its exact meaning.

**The story**

- **Land revenue** was the **main income** of the state.
- **Taxes** were charged on **professions, marriages, salt, textiles and cattle**.
- **Farming was prosperous**; labourers were often paid in grain, and the pilgrim **Hsuen Tsang** noted how fertile the land was.
- **Brahmadeya** villages — tax-free land given to Brahmins — spread education and religion.
- At first people used **barter** (goods for goods); later the Pallavas issued **gold and silver coins** to help trade.
- Merchants formed guilds called **Manigramam**; special **Eripatti** (tank lands) were set aside so their income maintained the village irrigation tanks.

**Why it matters:** Tank-maintenance lands (Eripatti) show how closely the economy and irrigation were tied together in the dry south.

**Terms explained**

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Brahmadeya | Tax-free land granted to Brahmins |
| Manigramam | A merchant guild (traders' association) |
| Eripatti | "Tank land" whose income maintained a village irrigation tank |
| Barter | Exchanging goods directly, without money |

**Don't confuse:** **Brahmadeya** = land to Brahmins; **Devadana** = land to temples; **Eripatti** = land for tanks. Three different grants.

**Remember it:** **Brahma**deya → **Brahmins**; **Mani**gramam → **merchants**; **Eri** (Tamil for tank) → **tank** lands.

**TL;DR**
- Land revenue was the primary income; small taxes on professions, marriages, salt, textiles, cattle.
- Prosperous farming; labourers paid in kind.
- Brahmadeya = tax-free land to Brahmins.
- Barter gave way to gold and silver coins.
- Manigramam = merchant guilds; Eripatti = tank-maintenance lands.
keyPoints: Land revenue was the primary income; taxes on professions, marriages, salt, textiles, cattle.
Prosperous agriculture; labourers paid in kind (noted by Hsuen Tsang).
Brahmadeya = tax-free villages granted to Brahmins.
Barter gave way to gold and silver coinage to boost trade.
Manigramam = merchant guilds; Eripatti = tank lands funding village tanks.
items.mnemonic: Pallava economy: land revenue core → Brahmadeya grants → Manigramam guilds → Eripatti tank-lands.

items.title: Society, Religion, Literature & Decline of the Pallavas
items.body:
### Society, Religion, Literature & Decline of the Pallavas

**In one line:** Under the Pallavas, Hindu devotional worship (Bhakti) surged while Buddhism and Jainism faded — and after long wars drained the dynasty, the last Pallava king fell to the rising Cholas.

**Why it is asked:** The Bhakti saints (Alvars and Nayanars) and the "who ended Pallava rule?" fact are both common questions.

**The story**

**Religion and the Bhakti surge**
- Pallava kings supported **Saivism (Shiva)** and **Vaishnavism (Vishnu)**, while **Buddhism and Jainism slowly declined**.
- The **Bhakti movement** was spread by two groups of Tamil saint-poets: the **Alvars** (devotees of **Vishnu**) and the **Nayanars** (devotees of **Shiva**). Their hymns fill works like the *Nalayira Divya Prabandham* and the *Tirumurai*.
- The philosopher **Adi Shankaracharya** strengthened **Advaita** (non-dualist) philosophy, further reducing Buddhist and Jain influence.

**Arts and literature**
- In **Sanskrit**, Mahendravarman I wrote the **Mattavilasa Prahasana**; music and dance were encouraged, and the **Chittannavasal frescoes** preserve Pallava painting.

**Decline**
- **Constant wars** with the Chalukyas and Pandyas drained resources, and the Chalukyas even **plundered Kanchipuram**.
- The last Pallava king, **Aparajitavarman**, was **defeated by the Chola king Aditya I** in the late 9th century CE — ending Pallava rule and beginning **Chola dominance**.

**Why it matters:** The Bhakti movement reshaped South Indian religion for centuries, and the Pallava fall marks the handover of power to the Cholas.

**Terms explained**

- **Bhakti** — loving personal devotion to a god, through hymns rather than costly ritual.
- **Alvars / Nayanars** — Tamil saint-poets of Vishnu / Shiva.
- **Advaita** — the philosophy that the soul and the ultimate reality are one.

**Don't confuse:** **Alvars = Vishnu**, **Nayanars = Shiva**. Questions often reverse this pair.

**Remember it:** **A**lvars → **A** for... think "Alvar adores Vishnu"; Nayanar → Shiva. Pallavas end when **A**parajitavarman loses to **A**ditya I.

**TL;DR**
- Kings favoured Saivism and Vaishnavism; Buddhism and Jainism declined.
- Bhakti spread by Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva).
- Adi Shankaracharya reinforced Advaita philosophy.
- Mattavilasa Prahasana (Sanskrit); Chittannavasal frescoes (painting).
- Last Pallava Aparajitavarman defeated by Chola Aditya I — rise of the Cholas.
keyPoints: Kings favoured Saivism and Vaishnavism; Buddhism and Jainism declined.
Bhakti spread by Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva) in Tamil.
Adi Shankaracharya reinforced Advaita philosophy.
Mattavilasa Prahasana (Sanskrit); Chittannavasal frescoes (painting).
Aparajitavarman, the last Pallava, was defeated by Chola Aditya I — rise of the Cholas.
items.mnemonic: Pallava twilight: Bhakti of Alvars & Nayanars at their temples → Kanchi plundered → last king Aparajitavarman falls to Chola Aditya I.

items.title: Pulakeshin II — Diplomacy, Navy & Chalukya Precision Facts (PYQ)
items.body:
### Pulakeshin II — Diplomacy, Navy & Chalukya Precision Facts

**In one line:** Beyond his wars, Pulakeshin II was a diplomat with a navy who exchanged envoys with Persia — and the Chalukya state was more centralised than the village-run Pallava and Chola states.

**Why it is asked:** These precise "nugget" facts (Persian embassy, Ajanta mural, 100-ship navy, centralised rule) are exactly the discriminators examiners use in statement questions.

**The story**

- **Persian (Sasanian) embassy:** Pulakeshin II exchanged envoys with the Sasanian (Persian) emperor **Khusrau II** around **625 CE**. The welcome of a **Persian embassy is famously shown in a mural at Ajanta (Cave 1)**.
- **Naval power:** the Badami Chalukyas kept a **strong navy of about 100 ships** along the western coast.
- **Founder's claim:** the dynasty's founder **Pulakeshin I** fortified Vatapi and performed the **Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice)** to declare full sovereignty.
- **Administration contrast:** Chalukya rule was comparatively **centralised** — it did **not** give the strong village self-government seen under the Pallavas and later the Cholas (a common discrimination point).
- **Chinese testimony:** the pilgrim **Hiuen-Tsang** visited and praised the just rule of the Deccan king.

**Why it matters:** The Persian contact and the navy show the Chalukyas were a connected maritime power, not just a land kingdom.

**Terms explained**

- **Sasanian** — the Persian (Iranian) empire of that era.
- **Ashvamedha** — the Vedic horse sacrifice a king performed to proclaim supreme sovereignty.
- **Centralised** — power kept at the top, rather than shared with self-governing villages.

**Don't confuse:** **Pulakeshin I** (founder, did the Ashvamedha) is not **Pulakeshin II** (the greatest king, Persian embassy, stopped Harsha).

**Remember it:** Pulakeshin II = **Persia + navy**; Chalukya rule = **centralised** (unlike Pallava/Chola villages).

**TL;DR**
- Pulakeshin II exchanged embassies with the Sasanian emperor Khusrau II (about 625 CE); shown in an Ajanta Cave 1 mural.
- Badami Chalukyas kept a navy of about 100 ships.
- Founder Pulakeshin I fortified Vatapi and performed the Ashvamedha.
- Chalukya rule was centralised — unlike Pallava/Chola village autonomy.
- Hiuen-Tsang visited and praised the Deccan kingdom.
keyPoints: Pulakeshin II exchanged embassies with the Sasanian emperor Khusrau II (about 625 CE); shown in an Ajanta Cave 1 mural.
The Badami Chalukyas kept a strong navy of about 100 ships.
Pulakeshin I, the founder, fortified Vatapi and performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Chalukya administration was relatively centralised — unlike the village autonomy of the Pallavas/Cholas.
Hiuen-Tsang visited and praised Pulakeshin II's Deccan kingdom.
items.source: standard historical record — Aihole inscription, Ajanta Cave 1 Persian-embassy mural, Hiuen-Tsang's account of the Deccan

items.title: For Mains — Pallavas & Chalukyas (post-Gupta South India)
items.body:
## For Mains — Pallavas & Chalukyas

This subtopic feeds **Mains Paper-II clause M2-2** ("Pallavas, Chalukyas, Cholas; Delhi Sultanate; Islam; Bhakti & Sufi"). Mains answers must go beyond king-lists to analyse **state formation, cultural synthesis and legacy** in post-Gupta South India.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Political | Pallava–Chalukya "balance of power"; the Narmada as the north–south line (Pulakeshin II vs Harsha) |
| Administration | Pallava village self-government (Sabha, Urar, Kottam) vs the more centralised Chalukya state |
| Art & architecture | Birth of the Dravidian style; rock-cut to structural evolution; Vesara synthesis |
| Religion & society | Bhakti surge (Alvars, Nayanars), Adi Shankara's Advaita, decline of Buddhism/Jainism |
| Economy | Land grants (Brahmadeya), guilds (Manigramam), tank irrigation (Eripatti) |
| Legacy / way forward | Templates inherited by the Cholas; today's UNESCO conservation at Mamallapuram & Pattadakal |

**Data points / anchors to quote**
- **Aihole inscription (634 CE)** of **Ravikirti** — a model prashasti and chief source for Chalukya power.
- **Hsuen Tsang at Kanchi (642 CE)** — foreign testimony to Pallava prosperity.
- **UNESCO World Heritage Sites:** the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram and the temples at Pattadakal.
- **Pulakeshin II–Khusrau II embassy** (about 625 CE) — Deccan's maritime, diplomatic reach.

**AP angle:** The Pallavas rose partly from **south Andhra**, and the contemporary **Vishnukundins and Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** carried the same temple and Telugu-land culture into Andhra — a natural bridge to AP ancient history.

**Use in answers**
- *Example:* contrast Pallava village democracy with Chalukya centralisation to answer "state formation in early medieval South India".
- *Quote:* the Aihole prashasti to show inscriptions as history.
- *Diagram idea:* a simple timeline bar — Pullalur (Pallava loss) → Vatapi sacked (Pallava revenge) → Rajasimha's peace → Aditya I ends the Pallavas.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-II clause M2-2 (Pallavas, Chalukyas, Bhakti).
Core analytical axis: Pallava village self-government vs centralised Chalukya state.
Art thesis: birth of Dravidian style and Vesara synthesis; rock-cut to structural evolution.
Anchors: Aihole inscription (634 CE, Ravikirti), Hsuen Tsang (642 CE), UNESCO Mamallapuram & Pattadakal.
AP angle: Vishnukundins and Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi extend the culture into Andhra.
